newsitem.title: GERMANY: Top aide says Kohl can go on and on as chancellor.
newsitem.headline: Top aide says Kohl can go on and on as chancellor.

text.p: Helmut Kohl's presumed crown prince said in an interview released on Tuesday that the German chancellor could go on and on in office, and that the question of whether he runs again would be settled "at the right time".

Wolfgang Schaeuble, the powerful parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats, triggered a wave of speculation about Kohl's future in January when he said the chancellery was a temptation he would probably not resist if the chance arose.

But in an interview with the weekly Die Zeit released ahead of publication on Thursday, Schaeuble sought to play down the idea that Kohl, chancellor for more than 14 years, might not run in next year's general election.
He said Germans would be wise to vote for Kohl again. Asked if he was referring to 1998, Schaeuble replied: "Well, whenever. In 1998, or in 2002 or 2006."

Die Zeit asked jokingly if this would be the start of a new monarchy, the kind of question that was asked last October when Kohl, 66, overtook post-war chancellor Konrad Adenauer to become Germany's longest-serving head of government this century.
"Rubbish!" replied Schaeuble. "He's not even as old now as Adenauer was when he first became chancellor."

Since last October, the monument that Kohl had become has taken some hard knocks as unemployment has soared and major tax and pensions reform projects billed as election-winners have struggled to get off the ground.

In February he added to the speculation about his future when he said he would wait until after a European Union reform summit in Amsterdam in June before deciding whether or not to run for chancellor again in 1998.
For the first time in years, he seemed to lose his iron grip on dissent within the party as a number of younger CDU officials dared to criticise what they saw as a lack of drive at the top.

But he doggedly ignored pressure from political allies and leading commentators alike to commit himself to an early announcement on his political future, perhaps in April after he returns from an annual contemplative Easter holiday in Austria.

Schaeuble argued that the reforms -- of which he is widely sen as the principal architect -- were making solid progress, and said he did not believe the leadership issue was causing as much of a stir in Kohl's party as the interviewer presumed.
"I believe the matter (of who runs for chancellor) will all be settled in good time," Schaeuble said.
